PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 38 — Lesson 62: Comprehensive Health History, General Survey & Vital Signs

FNP-level goal: Perform a patient-centered, reproducible opening assessment that identifies instability, captures diagnostic context, obtains accurate vital signs, and turns history and general-survey data into a safe plan for focused examination, testing, follow-up, or escalation.

Learning Objectives

  • Organize a comprehensive history without losing the patient’s chief concern or narrative.
  • Use the general survey and vital signs as diagnostic data rather than intake formalities.
  • Recognize when repeat, manual, orthostatic, ambulatory, or home measurements add useful information.
  • Identify measurement error and avoid treating a potentially inaccurate vital sign as a definitive diagnosis.
  • Integrate medication, allergy, social, sexual, reproductive, family, functional, and behavioral-health history into risk assessment.
  • Recognize red flags requiring immediate emergency evaluation rather than a prolonged outpatient assessment.

Part 1 — The Opening Minute Is Clinical Data

Before the formal history begins, observe the patient’s appearance, work of breathing, posture, mobility, speech, affect, hydration, skin color, level of distress, and ability to participate. This is the general survey. A patient who is pale, diaphoretic, confused, unable to speak in full sentences, newly weak, or struggling to transfer safely needs a different pace and setting than a comfortable patient with stable chronic symptoms.

Begin with privacy, consent, preferred name/pronouns when appropriate, and an agenda. An opening question such as “What is the most important thing you want us to address today?” helps prevent a technically complete but clinically irrelevant encounter. Avoid assuming that a quiet patient is stable or that an anxious patient’s symptoms are benign; observe, ask, measure, and reassess.

Part 2 — Chief Concern, HPI, and Functional Impact

The chief concern records why the patient seeks care, ideally in their own words. The history of present illness explains the timeline and context: onset, location, duration, character, severity, timing, triggers, relieving factors, associated symptoms, prior episodes, prior evaluation, treatment response, and meaningful negatives. For complex visits, confirm which problem is primary and identify issues that cannot safely wait.

Always ask what the symptom prevents the patient from doing. Functional change is often more revealing than a numerical symptom score: new inability to walk a usual distance, climb stairs, work, sleep, eat, take medicines, or perform self-care may signal severity even when the patient minimizes pain. Compare with the patient’s baseline, not with a generic expectation for age.

Part 3 — Past History Is a Risk Map

Medical, surgical, obstetric/gynecologic, psychiatric, and hospitalization history changes probability and prescribing safety. Ask about diagnoses and complications, prior procedures, transfusions, falls, fractures, cancer, thrombosis, heart or lung disease, kidney/liver disease, diabetes, immune compromise, and recent emergency or inpatient care. Determine what has changed since the last visit; an old problem list may not reflect the current clinical picture.

Family history is most useful when it identifies early or clustering disease that changes screening or suspicion: premature cardiovascular disease, sudden unexplained death, cancer patterns, inherited lipid disorders, thrombosis, diabetes, psychiatric illness, or known genetic conditions. It is not a ritual recitation of every relative’s diagnosis.

Part 4 — Medication, Allergy, and Substance Histories Prevent Harm

Medication reconciliation means more than comparing a list. For each prescription, over-the-counter product, vitamin, supplement, injection, inhaler, topical product, and as-needed medicine, clarify the exact name, dose, route, schedule, indication, prescriber, adherence, benefit, adverse effects, and recent changes. Ask how the patient actually takes it. Duplicate ingredients, old lists, shared medicines, cost-related dose skipping, and misunderstood instructions are common sources of diagnostic and medication error.

Document the reaction—not just the word “allergy.” A rash, anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous reaction, intolerance, nausea, headache, or lack of effect have different implications. Ask about alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, stimulants, opioids, sedatives, and other substances in a nonjudgmental way because exposure, withdrawal, interaction, and safety risks can mimic or complicate disease.

Part 5 — Social, Sexual, Reproductive, and Behavioral Health Are Core Data

Housing, food access, transportation, literacy, work schedule, caregiving, insurance, immigration-related concerns, safety, and ability to obtain medicines influence whether a plan can work. Ask respectfully about intimate-partner violence, coercion, and safety when clinically appropriate and provide private opportunities to respond. A patient who cannot afford an inhaler, travel to imaging, or safely follow up needs a different plan than one who can.

Sexual and reproductive history should be inclusive and related to the clinical question: pregnancy potential, contraception, menstrual pattern, fertility goals, STI exposure, anatomy, partners, and practices when relevant. Pregnancy status can change medication safety, imaging choices, differential diagnosis, and urgency. Depression, anxiety, trauma, sleep, cognition, substance use, and suicidal thoughts may be central to the presenting concern rather than an optional separate topic.

Part 6 — Vital Signs Are Measurements, Not Truths

Temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, pain, height/weight when relevant, and mental-status observation are powerful data points. Each can be inaccurate, transient, or clinically misleading if collected without context. Repeat an unexpected value. Confirm that the patient is not in acute exertion, severe pain, or distress when interpreting a chronic-management reading. Compare with baseline and with the patient’s appearance.

Respiratory rate and oxygenation should be interpreted together with work of breathing, speech, mental status, and trend. A normal pulse-oximeter value does not rule out serious disease, and a low value must be checked for signal quality, perfusion, device limitation, and the patient’s clinical condition. Do not let a single reassuring number override visible respiratory distress, cyanosis, altered mentation, or exhaustion.

Part 7 — Accurate Blood Pressure Is a Clinical Skill

Before treating an elevated or unexpectedly low blood pressure, verify technique. The patient should be appropriately prepared and seated with back supported, feet flat and uncrossed, the arm supported at heart level, the cuff on bare skin and correctly sized, and no conversation during measurement. Recent caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, exercise, a full bladder, anxiety, pain, and an unsupported arm can alter readings.

Repeat concerning readings using sound technique and consider both arms or manual confirmation when appropriate. One office measurement does not by itself establish a chronic diagnosis or explain acute symptoms. Home or ambulatory readings can help clarify white-coat effect, masked hypertension, or response to therapy when used with a validated device and a structured log. Severe elevation accompanied by acute neurologic symptoms, chest pain, pulmonary edema, visual change, encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, or other target-organ concern is an emergency assessment problem—not a routine medication-adjustment visit.

Part 8 — Orthostatic Assessment: Use It for the Right Patient

Orthostatic vital signs can be useful for selected patients with dizziness, presyncope/syncope, weakness, falls, suspected volume loss, blood loss, autonomic symptoms, medication effects, or postural complaints. Record symptoms and heart rate as well as blood pressure; use a consistent position sequence and local protocol. A sustained fall in blood pressure after standing can support orthostatic hypotension, but results do not independently establish the cause.

Interpret the pattern with hydration, bleeding risk, infection, medication exposure, neuropathy, cardiac disease, anemia, and neurologic symptoms. Do not force a frail, unstable, or symptomatic patient to stand just to complete a measurement. If the patient is hypotensive, actively bleeding, severely dehydrated, has syncope with high-risk features, chest pain, new neurologic deficits, or cannot stand safely, prioritize stabilization and emergency evaluation.

Part 9 — Red Flags That Change the Visit Immediately

Stop and escalate when findings suggest compromised airway, breathing, circulation, or brain function: severe respiratory distress, low perfusion, cyanosis, new confusion, syncope with instability, focal neurologic deficit, severe chest pain, active major bleeding, suspected sepsis, severe allergic reaction, rapidly progressive weakness, or concern for self-harm/violence. A complete outpatient history is not more important than timely transfer.

Use the general survey, vital signs, history, and focused examination together. A patient can have a reassuring blood pressure and still have a stroke, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, ectopic pregnancy, GI bleed, or another emergency. Conversely, an isolated abnormal measurement may be technical or temporary. The FNP skill is recognizing when the whole picture is unsafe.

Part 10 — Documentation That Supports Continuity and Safety

Document the history and assessment in a way that allows another clinician to understand the patient’s baseline, symptom trajectory, key risk factors, meaningful positives/negatives, vital-sign context, differential, and disposition. Record what was repeated or verified, who owns pending results, when follow-up will occur, and what return precautions were explained.

High-quality documentation is not a longer note. It is a clear record of reasoning and patient communication. Avoid copying forward old diagnoses, medication lists, or normal examination language when they were not reviewed or are no longer accurate.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: A “Routine” Blood-Pressure Follow-up

A 68-year-old arrives for hypertension follow-up with a blood pressure of 184/98. They walked quickly from the parking lot, drank coffee, report new shortness of breath when lying down, and have bilateral leg swelling.

FNP reasoning: repeat the blood pressure with correct technique, but do not frame this only as a number. The new dyspnea and edema require assessment for congestion, heart failure, renal disease, medication effects, and other causes. Determine stability and urgency before simply increasing an outpatient antihypertensive dose.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Dizziness After Medication Changes

A 79-year-old reports dizziness on standing and two recent falls after several medication changes. They have poor oral intake and take a diuretic, antihypertensive, sedative, and diabetes medication.

FNP reasoning: assess injury, neurologic and cardiac red flags, hydration, glucose, medication timing, and functional safety. Orthostatic vital signs may be useful if safe to obtain, but the result must be integrated with the broader risk of falls, hypoglycemia, arrhythmia, volume depletion, and polypharmacy. A medication list is not a plan until it is reconciled with how the patient is actually taking it.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: The Incomplete Medication List

A patient with abdominal pain says they take “nothing.” When asked specifically, they report daily ibuprofen, an over-the-counter sleep aid, a weight-loss supplement, and a borrowed acid-suppression medicine.

FNP reasoning: the differential and medication-safety plan have changed. NSAID exposure can affect GI, kidney, and bleeding risk; supplements may have adverse effects or interactions. Complete reconciliation is diagnostic work, not clerical work.

FNP Comprehensive-Assessment Framework

  1. Observe first: general survey, distress, function, safety, and stability.
  2. Set the agenda: patient priorities, chief concern, urgent issues, and visit constraints.
  3. Build the story: timeline, context, associated symptoms, function, and meaningful negatives.
  4. Map risk: medical/family history, medications, allergy reactions, substances, social determinants, pregnancy potential, and mental health.
  5. Validate measurements: correct technique, repeat unexpected vital signs, and compare with baseline/appearance.
  6. Escalate early: do not delay emergency care to finish a complete outpatient template.
  7. Close the loop: document reasoning, pending work, follow-up ownership, and explicit return precautions.

High-Yield Summary

General survey: immediate diagnostic data about appearance, distress, function, and stability.
HPI: timeline + context + associated features + functional change, not a symptom checklist alone.
Medication reconciliation: exact use, not merely the chart list; include OTCs, supplements, and substances.
Vital signs: interpret technique, trend, baseline, and the patient—not a number in isolation.
Blood pressure: verify cuff, position, rest, and repeat abnormal values before chronic treatment decisions.
Orthostatics: selective tool for postural symptoms/volume risk; never delay stabilization or create a fall risk.
FNP standard: combine patient narrative, general survey, accurate measurement, risk context, and safety-netting into one coherent plan.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Comprehensive assessment, vital-sign technique, diagnostic testing, emergency triage, medication decisions, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local policy, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
